comparison: Perfect agreement on IL10 protein loss and functional consequences (C6-C9). Both evaluations support the ELISA/Griess assay findings showing complete loss in HOM, partial loss in HET, lack of dosage compensation, and effects on nitric oxide production. OpenEval and peer reviewers both find evidence convincing.

Perfect agreement on microbiome findings (C15-C20). Both evaluations accept the 16S rDNA sequencing data, LEfSe analysis, PCA results (R²=0.25, p=0.017), and conclusion that IL10 regulates microbiome composition. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on vaccine response findings (C24-C26). Both evaluations support the ELISA data showing vaccine-specific differences in antibody responses. Peer review implicitly accepts these findings as part of overall immune characterization, while OpenEval notes biological significance remains unclear.

Perfect agreement on broader implications (C75-C76). Both evaluations affirm the trade-off between enhanced pathogen clearance and increased inflammation/pathology, and recognize implications for poultry disease control strategies. Reviewers explicitly noted applicability to livestock industry.

Strong agreement on knockout model generation (C1-C5 vs C2-C5). OpenEval includes C1 (overall methodology claim) while peer review focuses on C2-C5 (molecular characterization and inheritance). Both evaluations fully support the CRISPR/PGC methodology and germline transmission without criticism.

Strong agreement on absence of spontaneous colitis (C10-C14, C21-C23). OpenEval R3 addresses C10-C14 while peer R3 includes environmental effects C21-C23. Both highlight this as a major finding distinguishing chickens from mouse models. All reviewers treated this species difference as a key result.

Agreement on environmental modulation findings (C21-C23). OpenEval R5 specifically addresses growth and histopathology differences between SPF and conventional environments. Peer R3 groups these claims with the broader colitis findings (C10-C14), accepting environmental effects as part of the phenotypic characterization.

Strong agreement on bacterial challenge findings (C27-C31, C36 vs C27-C36, C49). OpenEval focuses on C. jejuni and summary claims, while peer review encompasses both bacterial pathogens. Both accept enhanced pathogen clearance with elevated inflammation and acknowledge variability between cohorts.

Agreement on Salmonella challenge findings (C32-C35). OpenEval R8 specifically addresses S. Typhimurium temporal progression. Peer R6 groups these with broader bacterial challenge results (C27-C36, C49), accepting the temporal dynamics from marginal effects at 1 week to significant clearance at 2 weeks.

Strong agreement on dose-dependent effects and trade-offs (C38-C42 vs C38-C42, C43-C47, C50). OpenEval R9 focuses on contrasting phenotypes between HOM and HET. Peer R7 encompasses both bacterial and parasitic challenges, highlighting the central finding of pathogen clearance vs tissue damage trade-off.

Agreement on Eimeria challenge findings (C43-C47). OpenEval R10 addresses parasitic infection time-course data. Peer R7 groups these with bacterial challenges (C38-C50), accepting the comprehensive evidence for enhanced clearance with increased inflammation across all pathogens tested.

Agreement on summary of bacterial challenge findings (C48-C51, with C49 overlap). OpenEval R11 summarizes all challenge experiments. Peer R6 addresses bacterial challenges specifically. Both accept the consistent pattern of enhanced clearance with increased inflammation, though peer review groups findings differently.

Agreement on overall challenge experiment conclusions (C48-C51, with C50 overlap). OpenEval R11 provides comprehensive summary across all pathogens. Peer R7 emphasizes dose-dependent effects and trade-offs. Both evaluations support the integrated findings from bacterial and parasitic infections.

Agreement on differential genotype effects (C48-C51, with C51 overlap). OpenEval R11 summarizes major findings including dose-dependent effects. Peer R8 implicitly accepts differential effects between genotypes as part of overall conclusions. Both support the pattern across all challenge experiments.

Agreement on speculative/interpretive claims (C62-C63 vs C62-C65, C67, C73-C74). OpenEval rates C62-C63 as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature and lack of direct causal testing. Peer review accepts these interpretive claims as appropriate for Discussion section, not challenging the speculation about microbiome-colitis relationship or commercial applicability.

Agreement on C. jejuni contextualization (C64-C65). OpenEval supports these claims as appropriate literature context. Peer R10 groups with other interpretive claims, accepting the acknowledgment of variability and species differences without challenge.

Agreement on mammalian literature context (C66-C67). OpenEval supports C66-C67 as appropriate contextualization with acknowledgment of uncertainty about avian applicability. Peer R10 accepts discussion of species differences, noting this is the first conclusive demonstration in avian models.

Agreement on intervention study context (C68, C70-C72). OpenEval supports these claims as appropriate summary of prior work and comparison between complete knockout and partial reduction. Peer R10 implicitly accepts this contextualization as part of overall discussion framework.

Agreement on speculative predictions (C73-C74). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting these are speculative predictions about untested scenarios representing future work. Peer R10 accepts these as appropriate speculative claims for Discussion section without challenge.

OpenEval R12 addresses background claims on mammalian IL10 biology (C52-C59). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These literature context claims were not explicitly discussed by peer reviewers, though they form the foundation for interpreting the chicken studies.

OpenEval R13 addresses chicken IL10 sequence conservation and rationale (C60-C61). No corresponding peer review evaluation found. Peer reviewers did not explicitly comment on these foundational claims establishing the basis for investigating IL10 function in chickens.
